questions.q: What kind of scenario is Northfield Retail, as described in this case study?
options: An illustrative, fictional scenario built to make a common failure pattern concrete, not a real company
A real, publicly documented company whose platform rollout failed
An anonymized but factual account of an actual incident at a named client
A hypothetical the platform team at Northfield is currently living through in real time
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames Northfield Retail as illustrative and fictional, used to make a real and common pattern concrete without claiming it describes any actual company.

questions.q: What was the platform team's first real signal that adoption was low?
options: A developer-experience survey conducted before launch
Deployment frequency and lead time data gathered during the build
Low adoption itself, arriving roughly six months after launch
A direct complaint filed by an application team during the architecture review
questions.explain: Because there was no feedback loop before or during the build, the first real signal was low adoption itself, arriving months late -- the slowest and most expensive signal available.

questions.q: Why does mandated adoption fail to prove a platform is actually helping anyone?
options: Mandates are technically impossible to enforce through a catalog-info.yaml
It measures compliance -- services getting registered -- rather than value, since teams can register on paper while still running old processes underneath
Mandated adoption always increases deployment frequency immediately
A VP-issued mandate automatically fixes any golden-path mismatch
questions.explain: Teams registered their catalog-info.yaml to satisfy the mandate while quietly keeping old deploy scripts running, since the mandate covered registering, not actually using, the golden path.

questions.q: What was the deepest problem with Northfield's golden path template?
options: It had no monitoring dashboard wired in at all
It lacked a canary rollout strategy
It was missing automated rollback entirely
It was designed around stateless Node.js services and didn't fit the batch jobs and compliance-constrained services a meaningful share of real teams actually ran
questions.explain: The golden path matched the platform team's own comfortable assumptions about a typical service, not the actual shape of a meaningful share of Northfield's real workloads.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should happen when a team's service genuinely doesn't fit the first golden path?
options: The team should be pressured harder to force their service into the existing template
That mismatch should be treated as a signal to build a second template for that kind of work, not a reason to pressure the team into a bad fit
The team should be excluded from the platform entirely and ignored
The golden path should be deleted and every team should go back to copy-paste repos
questions.explain: Treating a mismatch as a signal to build a second, better-fitting template is what 'platform as a product' actually looks like in practice -- forcing a bad fit is the opposite.
